10674-how-to-use-your-mind-a-psychology-:
Harry D. Kitson, a professor of psychology at Indiana University, wrote How to Use Your Mind in 1921 as a manual for students and teachers. It treats study as a skill that can be taught, especially in high school and the lower grades, where habits of attention are first set. Kitson argues that colleges receive students whose study habits are already fixed, for good or ill.

The book explains how to focus, remember, read with purpose, and manage time, drawing on early research in learning. Teachers get guidance for supervising study, and students get practical steps rather than vague advice. Modern readers will find a clear, early statement of study skills, much of it still familiar today.
11067-reform-cookery-book-4th-edition-up:
This fourth edition of the Reform Cookery Book presents up-to-date health cookery for vegetarian households, with practical recipes and a directory of the health-food trade. Its front matter lists stockists across Scotland, including the Edinburgh Health Foods Depot at 40 Hanover Street, carrying all Wallace goods, and Glasgow's Health Food Supply Company, wholesale and retail dealers.

Recipes give plain, usable directions: fried artichokes are parboiled, dipped in egg, tossed in crumbs or crumbs and grated cheese, and fried in smoking hot fat. Stewed celery is soaked in vinegar and water, then parboiled. Brand goods such as Artox bread and biscuits, Hovis, and vegetable meats like Vejola and Nutmeatose recur throughout, tying recipes to the shops that sold them.
12806-dick-prescott-s-third-year-at-west:
Dick Prescott returns to West Point for his third year after a summer furlough in his home town. Back in cadet grey, he faces a turnback's scheme, a lawyer's surprise, and a traitor in the riding hall, with football against Lehigh for relief. Old friends Greg Holmes, Dave Darrin, and Dan Dalzell cross his path.

The core test is honour under pressure: Dick must stand firm when enemies plot in the dark and a friend's name is at stake. Hancock mixes academy routine with mystery and sport in his usual clean style. The book suits young readers who follow Dick's rise from Gridley schoolboy to officer.
13170-the-lake-of-the-sky-lake-tahoe-in-:
George Wharton James's Lake of the Sky covers Lake Tahoe in the high Sierras of California and Nevada, with history, Indians, discovery by Frémont, legend, geology, and resorts. Its subtitle promises fishing, hunting, flowers, birds, trees, and chaparral, with a full account of the Tahoe National Forest. James, author of books on Arizona and New Mexico, writes as a guide and enthusiast.

He describes moraines near Mount Tallac, polished canyon floors from glaciation, and a breakfast spoiled by gale winds that sent flames up arms and rocks. A snowdrift marks a landmark at seven in the morning, while a rowboat crosses the bay below. The book is a thick, loving handbook to Tahoe, meant for travelers, campers, and summer residents.
14746-a-dialoge-or-communication-of-two-:
Printed in early modern spelling, this dialogue presents a conversation in the manner of Desiderius Erasmus on the pilgrimage of pure devotion. Two speakers talk through what a pilgrimage should mean, rather than treating the road itself as the whole of faith.

Scripture, prayer and the inner life run through their exchange. The speakers return to promises of Christ, the love between Father and Son, and the kingdom of God as described in holy writing. Outward forms are weighed against inward change, so the work reads as a Reformation-era case for devotion rooted in belief and conduct, not in travel alone.
18553-from-isolation-to-leadership-revis:
John Holladay Latané wrote this review of American foreign policy. Latané was professor of American history and dean at Johns Hopkins University. Doubleday, Page published the revised book in 1922, with copyrights in 1918 and 1922. The book traces how the United States moved from isolation to leadership in world affairs.

Chapters take up the origin of isolation, the Monroe Doctrine, the open-door policy, Anglo-American relations, and the failure of neutrality. Later chapters cover the war aims of the United States, the Treaty of Versailles, and the Washington Conference, closing with America's new place among nations.
19821-the-nursery-no-103-july-1875-vol-x:
The Nursery was a monthly magazine for young children, printed in Boston. Number 103, July 1875, is volume eighteen of the run. Its publishers promise coming numbers to make little readers' eyes sparkle. No other magazine, they boast, can take its place with its audience. Canvassers are urged to start work with a will. Subscription selling kept such magazines alive.

Magazines for the very young were a new trade in 1875. Large type, pictures, and short pieces suited new readers. The Nursery came from the circle of John L. Shorey, its publisher. Bound volumes lived in family libraries for years. A single number preserves the era's nursery taste. Stories, verses, and booster talk share its pages.
24786-games-and-play-for-school-morale-a:
Arranged by Mel Sheppard and Anna Vaughan and issued by Community Service in 1920, this manual offers graded games for schools and neighborhoods. Its aim is school morale: play that brings a whole community together, builds good will, and fills idle hours with shared fun. Games are sorted by age and setting, from classroom rows to open yards.

Each game comes with plain rules, such as bean-bag relays where rows race to fill a circle and run back. Teachers get a ready stock of contests that need little gear. The book still reads as a practical handbook for anyone planning group play, recess, or a community evening.
27742-popular-education-for-the-use-of-p:
Ira Mayhew, Michigan's superintendent of public instruction, prepared this 1850 manual at the request of the state legislature, gathering his public lectures on popular education. It addresses parents, teachers, and young people of both sexes.

Mayhew argues that every child should receive a good common-school education, and he gives citizens and teachers practical direction for improving primary schools. The book stands as a mid-century statement of the common-school ideal: schooling as a public good, political as well as moral and religious. Mayhew had delivered much of the material as public lectures before the legislature asked for the book.
28077-friends-in-feathers-and-fur-and-ot:
James Johonnot's Friends in Feathers and Fur, and Other Neighbors, published in New York in 1885, is a natural-history reader for young folks. Johonnot introduces birds, beasts, and other neighbours in short, lively sketches, with pictures throughout. The book belongs to his Natural History Series, second book, issued by D. Appleton and Company.

Its opening argues that schooling should wake thought, not train children like speaking machines. The animal tales that follow teach habits, homes, and calls in plain words. Young readers learn to watch nature closely and to treat animals as neighbours, not merely as curiosities.
28130-the-nursery-february-1877-vol-xxi-:
The Nursery for February 1877, volume twenty-one, number two, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers from John L. Shorey. Its lead piece, Christmas Presents Made Here, follows Edwin, who uses a jig-saw gift to make brackets, shelves, and toy houses, giving many away and selling some to buy books. Other prose covers his dog Jack, a steamer, squirrels, and a first astronomy lesson.

Verse includes the sparrows' petition, Ensign Johnny, and the froggies' party, with Chipperee Chip set to music. Drawing lessons, a rescue, and tales of sheep and ravens round out the number. The issue blends work, kindness, and nature for small readers.
28138-the-nursery-october-1877-vol-xxii-:
The Nursery for October 1877, volume twenty-two, number four, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers from John L. Shorey. Its lead tale, The Parrot That Played Truant, follows Polly, pet of old Miss Dorothy Draper, who slips from an open cage and flies from tree to tree and lamp-post to lamp-post. Other prose covers ducks, chestnuts, alligators, and a faithful dog named Dandy.

Verse offers a baby's lay, pigs, a goose-drawing rhyme, and The White Owl, set to music. A spider family, a thrush, and a cat with a starling add nature notes. The issue keeps the magazine's gentle mix of pets, seasons, and small adventures.
33535-the-development-of-armor-piercing-:
Carlos De Zafra's Development of Armor-Piercing Shells, with suggestions for their improvement, published in 1915, traces how projectiles grew to meet modern warfare. De Zafra, a faculty lecturer at New York University, notes that shell-making advanced through experiments based at first more on theory than on any other branch of engineering. His history moves from wooden days to steel and science.

The study suits readers of military technology, offering a technical yet readable account of a deadly craft. Its tone is scholarly and practical, aimed at engineers and officers. For students of ordnance, it is a valuable source on how shells learned to pierce armor, and how they might pierce it better.
3821-the-roman-and-the-teuton-a-series-o:
Charles Kingsley delivered these Cambridge lectures on the fall of Rome and the rise of the Gothic peoples. The contents move from the forest children and the dying empire through the human deluge to Dietrich, the Gothic civilizer, and his end. Then come the nemesis of the Goths, the Lombard laws, and the popes. Max Muller, who supplies a preface, remembers Kingsley as a caged lion of a mind, striving for utterance.

Later lectures weigh the clergy and the heathen, the monk as civilizer, and the strategy of providence in history. Kingsley argues with energy and moral heat, favoring the Teuton as a fresh force against a tired empire. Students of the early Middle Ages will find a dated but stirring survey, best read as a Victorian mind wrestling with the birth of Europe.
7543-quotes-and-images-from-the-tales-an:
Jean de La Fontaine is best known for his fables, and this companion volume gathers short passages and pictures from his tales and novels instead. Those longer stories carry their own sly wit, quite apart from the animal fables. Lovers, monks, lawyers, and country folk fill the scenes. Each passage can be traced to its full story, so a sharp line can be read in context.

Read together, the passages sketch a storyteller who enjoyed exposing folly with a smile. Love, law, greed, and clerical pretense recur across them, often with a sting at the end. Village life and polite society both supply targets. It suits browsers who like short, pointed reading: a tale's wit in miniature, with the full story close at hand.
8896-outlines-of-universal-history-desig:
George Park Fisher, professor at Yale University, writes Outlines of Universal History as a textbook for more advanced pupils and for private reading. Inscribed to his daughter as a token of love and thankfulness. His preface states the aim plainly: a work suited to older students, neither too slight nor too detailed. The transcriber's note explains Fisher's device of different type sizes, preserved here by indenting the smallest type. Detail can sit beside the main narrative without breaking its current.

Ancient, medieval, and modern history unfold in a single, steady survey, from early civilizations through empires, churches, revolutions, and nations. Fisher's Yale textbook shaped American history teaching for decades. Readers wanting a one-volume outline, whether for study or for refreshing a general picture. Will find a clear, orderly narrative, dated in places but still useful as a framework for deeper reading.
a-dialoge-or-communication-of-two-person: Desiderius Erasmus stages a dialogue of two persons on the pilgrimage of pure devotion. Newly translated into English, the text keeps much of its original spelling and punctuation. The speakers discuss true devotion against the outward show of pilgrimage. Erasmus writes with wit and reforming purpose in this early humanist dialogue. The talk is short, clear, and full of wit for modern readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-fil:
Francesco Filelfo, born at Tolentino on 25 July 1398 and dead at Florence on 31 July 1481, was a humanist whose restless career carried Greek learning into Renaissance Italy. He taught at Padua by eighteen, then at Venice, and in 1419 became secretary to the Venetian consul-general at Constantinople. There he learned Greek under John Chrysoloras, married his teacher's daughter, served the emperor John Palaeologus on diplomatic missions, and gathered a great collection of Greek books.

Back in Italy he taught at Venice, Bologna, and Florence, where quarrels with Florentine scholars and hatred of the Medici forced him out in 1434. At Milan, Filippo Maria Visconti showered him with honours, and under Francesco Sforza he wrote the Sforziad, a Latin epic in sixteen books on Sforza's life. He left Milan in 1474 for a professorship at Rome, closing a life spent between courts, universities, and feuds.
dick-prescott-s-third-year-at-west-point:
Year three at West Point fills H. Irving Hancock's third Dick Prescott book, on standing firm for flag and honour. It opens on furlough in the old home town. Mrs Prescott shows off her tall son, Richard, to the new pastor's wife with open pride.

Football fills much of the year, with a battle against Lehigh. After practice Brayton names the Army team for the morrow: Prescott at left end, Holmes at left tackle, and Haynes in reserve. A turnback scheme, a traitor of the riding hall, and a man moving in a dark room add plot. The degree of Coventry is pronounced in a late chapter. Honour, sport, and class feeling carry the book.
doe-osti-2571926-radiation-damage-effect:
Final technical report from the University of Wisconsin–Madison covers July 2020 to June 2023, with an extension to 2024. Izabela Szlufarska led the work, with Dane Morgan and Adrien Couet. The subject is radiation damage in beryllium. Beryllium is a leading candidate for beam windows and targets in next-generation proton accelerators such as the Long Baseline Neutrino Facility. Protons at one to one hundred gigaelectronvolts hammer such parts, and the damage decides how long they last.

Radiation knocks atoms loose and breeds helium inside the metal. At high temperatures the helium gathers into bubbles that swell the part and ease cracking. At low temperatures, defects pile up instead, hardening the metal and cutting its ductility. The team built a cluster dynamics model that predicts how helium bubbles form and grow with temperature and dose. Dual-beam experiments with low-energy protons supplied the data used to check the model.
doe-osti-2572456-summary-of-dm1200-wesp-:
Report HFO-72229, also numbered VSL-06R6710-1, from the Vitreous State Laboratory of the Catholic University of America, was published in July 2006 and released in July 2025. Authors K. S. Matlack, G. Diener, I. L. Pegg, M. Brandys, T. Bardakci, and W. Gong compile the history and performance of the DM1200 wet electrostatic precipitator. The unit cleans particulate-laden off-gas in Hanford's nuclear waste vitrification research.

Sections describe how the precipitator works, its specifications, and the design of its particle removal, electrical, and liquid removal systems. A summary of testing then walks through objectives, test exceptions, and research testing conditions. Results are scored against the original objectives, with notes on the simulants used in place of real waste. Quality requirements and open issues close the summary, along with follow-on tests the authors judged necessary.
doe-osti-2584732-probabilistic-seismic-h:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2006187, dated September 2025, presents a probabilistic seismic hazard analysis for Iraq. Wathiq Abdulnaby leads a fourteen-author team from the University of Basrah, the University of Baghdad, the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, and other institutions. The study updates Iraq's earthquake catalog and the ground motion data used to judge building risk.

The updated catalog covers 1900 through 2021 and holds more than 37,000 earthquakes, with moment magnitudes calculated directly for about 2,800 of them. Using data from about 30 strong motion stations, the team divided the study area into 20 seismic zones and ran OpenQuake analyses. Hazard maps show the highest risk near the Mandili-Badra-Teeb fault in eastern Iraq.
doe-osti-2586391-teamer-technical-suppor:
Thanh Toan Tran of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact on this final report, NREL/TP-5700-96030, issued in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-23-24078. Kim Nielsen and Jacob Schultz share credit for the project. Under the TEAMER program, the team gave technical support to the engineering firm Ramboll on numerical modeling of wave energy converters.

The work backed Task 10 of the Ocean Energy Systems collaboration, an international effort to verify and validate wave energy models against physical tests. Sandia's operator, National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, worked with NREL and Ramboll on fluid dynamics simulations in the open-source OpenFOAM package. Each case ran twice: once as a bare wave field, and once with a fixed sphere in place so forces and moments on the body could be compared with tank test results.
doe-osti-2586395-innovative-deep-water-m:
Matthew Hall of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact on this final report, NREL/TP-5000-95632, issued in August 2025 for CRADA number CRD-20-16882. Bruce Martin shares credit for the work. The DeepFarm project, led by Principle Power, designed mooring and anchoring systems for semi-submersible floating wind platforms in a deep-water commercial farm.

DeepFarm explored sharing anchors among platforms and used site conditions from the West Coast and Hawaii, at varied water depths, as case studies. NREL's role was modeling. It added a farm-level sea state capability to FAST.Farm so waves propagate across the whole farm, and it extended the MoorDyn mooring model to handle seabed friction and uneven seabed depth. NREL also ran its ORBIT model to price the resulting farm designs.
doe-osti-2588113-lower-cost-renewable-na:
Marca Doeff of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory was the technical contact for this CRADA final report, LBNL-2001690, dated August 1, 2025. Virginia Klausmeier of Sylvatex was the partner contact, through CalCharge LLC, under CRADA number FP00009902. The project sought a lower-cost, renewable nanoparticle platform to raise production of cathode material for lithium-ion batteries.

Sylvatex employees synthesized candidate cathode materials in Doeff's laboratories and at the Molecular Foundry, then benchmarked them against commercial materials in lithium half-cells. Work began with lithium iron phosphate, which avoids cobalt and its cost and mining concerns entirely. It later moved to nickel manganese cobalt oxides with low cobalt content. Synthesis methods were judged on energy use, carbon emissions, and wastewater as well as performance. The filing records 80,000 dollars of participant funding and lists no publications or subject inventions.
doe-osti-2589163-front-side-copper-metal:
Pauls Stradins of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5K00-96760, dated September 2025, with Ruvini Dharmadasa sharing credit. The partner, BERT Thin Films, makes copper metallization paste for silicon solar cells. Copper could replace costly silver in cell contacts. One fear blocks adoption: copper paste in a shared firing furnace might contaminate the line and degrade the silver cells made on it.

The CRADA tested that fear directly. BERT shipped 50 M6 blue PERC cells to NREL in August 2023. NREL printed silver paste on the fronts, kept a third as controls, and sent the rest back. BERT printed its copper paste on its cells, returning them in February 2024. With both cell types moving through the same equipment, the team could measure whether copper exposure harmed silver cell performance. The answer decides whether factories can try copper without dedicating a furnace to it.
doe-osti-2998424-visionary-virtual-intel:
VISIONARY, an artificial intelligence system for mining research literature, is presented by Oceane Bel, Sungmin Kim, Khushbu Agarwal, and co-authors in a September 2025 Pacific Northwest report. Instead of scanning all of science, the system works from a curated, domain-specific base of papers. Analysts use it to find where studies disagree with one another, since contradictions mark the questions worth testing next.

That targeted reading, the authors argue, produces sharper hypotheses than broad trawls through the literature. The name expands to Virtual Intelligence System for Optimizing Novel Analytical Research Yields, which states the goal plainly: more useful research questions per analyst hour. The report frames the system and its intended workflow for research teams drowning in publications, where the gap between two solid papers is often the real discovery waiting to be made.
doe-osti-3001937-efficient-and-selective:
Wenjin Cao, Natalie Isenberg, Grant Johnson and Samantha Johnson of PNNL study chemistry in droplets, in an October 2025 report. A charged nanodroplet is a strange reactor: cramped, stressed, with surfaces ruling the interior. Reactions inside, including amines capturing carbon dioxide, can run faster and more selectively than in bulk liquid. Harnessing that means predicting it.

An electrospray mass spectrometry platform ran the droplet reactor while a hybrid model learned from it. The model weds a physics based formulation of reaction and mass transfer kinetics, rate constants from density functional theory, and measured reactant and product levels. Bayesian inference fits the physics. A Gaussian process then absorbs the leftover mismatch, with uneven measurement noise handled by a parametric model. Multi objective optimisation steers experiments toward the most useful conditions. The conclusions present a self improving loop of instrument, model and optimiser.
doe-osti-3002997-evaluation-of-iec-62443:
Sheryl I. Drake and Christopher C. Lamb audit a cybersecurity standard in Sandia report SAND2025-13805, printed September 2025. The standard is IEC 62443, the main rulebook for industrial control system security. The test case is an electric grid substation model. The authors ask where the standard gives too little guidance for the risks substations actually face.

Gaps cluster around legacy gear and physical threats. Older remote terminal units and controllers may speak Modbus or DNP3 protocols that lack encryption, and the standard says little about retrofitting them. Tamper risks to monitoring systems get limited treatment. Recommendations include encrypted protocols with authentication, locked and tamper-proof enclosures, and cryptographic checks on firmware updates. Utility security teams are the intended readers.
doe-osti-3003229-5g-integrated-edge-comp:
Deepak K. Tosh and Shirley V. Moore of the University of Texas at El Paso deliver the final report for DOE grant DE-FE0032089, submitted November 17, 2025. The project ran from August 2021 to August 2025. It built a monitoring platform for coal-fired power plants that joins 5G wireless links with edge computing, small computers placed near the equipment they watch.

The framework runs distributed and federated machine learning to spot component anomalies in real time. Dynamic network slicing over 5G reserves bandwidth for the monitoring traffic. The design targets scalable, fault-tolerant operation inside industrial control environments, where a missed sensor failure can force an outage. The report closes the grant with the system's design and its test results. Plant operators and industrial computing researchers are the audience.
doe-osti-3005263-rpi-unstructured-meshin:
Mark Shephard of Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute reports the institute's work for the FASTMath SciDAC 5 applied math institute, under award SC0021285. FASTMath builds the mathematics software that big simulations stand on. RPI's share is unstructured meshing: dividing complex shapes into elements on exascale machines, fast and at scale. Partner SciDAC projects steered which tools got built.

Three threads stand out. PUMIPic-style hybrid mesh and particle infrastructure now underlies plasma turbulence, impurity transport, ice sheet, and neutronics codes. A coupling layer, PCMS, moves data between physics codes in memory, one-way or two-way. Mesh tally methods were extended for Monte Carlo transport. The report lists the gateway and conference outputs that carried the tools to users. It is a capstone for one institute partner, written for the program record.
doe-osti-3011291-randomized-federated-le:
Federated learning methods for nonsmooth, nonconvex, and hierarchical problems are developed in the final report for award DE-SC0023303. Farzad Yousefian of Rutgers led the work, with Uday Shanbhag as co-investigator. The project ran from September 2022 to August 2025, counting a no-cost extension year, with total costs of 400,000 dollars.

Three thrusts produced smoothing-enabled zeroth-order methods with provable bounds on communication, iteration, and sample counts. Inexact implicit variants cover the hierarchical cases. The work also gave early non-asymptotic rate analyses for stochastic programs with equilibrium constraints. Doctoral students at three universities trained on the project.
doe-osti-3014737-leveraging-arm-data-to-:
Using Atmospheric Radiation Measurement data to sharpen models of energy and security hazards is the topic of DOE/SC-ARM-26-004, dated January 2026. The report covers a two-part virtual workshop held on November 4 and 14, 2025, where ARM users and modelers compared notes on events that strain power and water systems. J. H. Mather of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory led the author team.

The hazards on the table include winter storms, freezing rain, wet snow loading, severe convection, flooding and landslides, wildfires, prolonged heat, and drought. Sessions weighed which ARM observations would most improve forecasts and planning models for each threat. The authors disclose that the discussion draft was generated from meeting notes with AI help, then reviewed and edited by the author team.
doe-osti-3018729-lessons-learned-from-si:
Kristopher L Kuhlman of Sandia, Jens Birkholzer and Patrick Dobson of Lawrence Berkeley, and Mahrez Ben Belfadhel distilled siting lessons in SAND2026-17151R, dated February 10, 2026. Their subject is deep geological disposal of spent fuel and high-level waste. Three national programs anchor the comparison. Germany and Switzerland each started from the whole country. Technical screening then narrowed the map toward a site. Canada took the other end of the spectrum. Its program began with extensive public engagement, and communities helped shape the siting process itself.

The report walks each program's steps, including Canada's initial screenings: 22 conducted, one community excluded. Screening criteria were applied with readily available information, in two to three months per community. Lessons concern sequencing as much as geology. The United States is restarting its own siting effort. This February 2026 synthesis hands the American program three worked examples, with their mistakes priced in.
doe-osti-3018749-an-overview-of-manufact:
Talia G Duffy of Sandia wrote this overview, SAND2026-16541, on manufacturing controls for systems that must work the first and only time. High-consequence, single-use systems cannot be tested as finished units; firing the product destroys it. Confidence has to come from the process instead. Duffy's survey begins with statistical quality control. Sampling plans, acceptance probabilities, and average total inspection are explained with their formulas. Rectifying inspection, where rejected lots get fully screened, is covered as a working option.

The overview connects those classic tools to the controls a production line actually runs. Lot definitions, inspection levels, and disposition rules translate statistics into floor practice. For weapons and space hardware alike, this is the standard bargain: sample the lot, control the process, certify the item. Duffy gives new quality engineers one map of that bargain. The report is an overview by design, pointing readers to the standards it summarizes.
doe-osti-3019909-transmission-line-based:
J Candy, B Illingworth, K Cantwell, S Lehman, and J Fowler of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory designed a damage sensor in LLNL-TR-2014442, updated October 28, 2025. The sensor is a transmission line interrogated by FMCW radar. Radar chirps travel the line; damage changes the line, and the reflections report it. The framework marries classical electromagnetic propagation theory to impact mechanics. That pairing lets the authors model how a collision evolves damage in space and time, and what the radar sees while it happens.

Detection statistics close the loop. The report derives detection probability for an adaptive threshold detector under Gaussian noise, and for a fixed-threshold variant. False alarm probabilities get parallel formulas. A sensor that cannot state its own error rates is a gadget, not an instrument. For structures facing high-velocity impacts, this design work offers continuous inspection. The transmission line becomes the thing watched and the watcher.
doe-osti-3019919-radiological-releases-f:
M D Shah of Oak Ridge National Laboratory examined sabotage effects for advanced reactors in ORNL/SPR-2026/4449, February 2026. Developers argue that robust fuels and inherent safety justify smaller security forces and emergency planning zones. Shah's analyses test the other side of that bargain. Sabotage-induced release scenarios were run beyond design basis, conservative, and produced very large release fractions. Those crude fractions had been applied as demonstrations. The report refines the consequence analysis for novel fuel forms under severe accidents.

Simulated variations included an anticipated transient without scram, with and without control rod insertion. Across the first 24 hours, maximum fuel temperature stayed below the cladding melting point. Strong negative feedback from Doppler broadening and fuel elongation did that work. For regulators, the message cuts both ways: conservative fractions overstate risk, but the physics of these fuels truly resists temperature excursion. Emergency planning debates can now cite computed behavior.
doe-osti-3022393-cybersecurity-incident-:
INL report INL/RPT-25-87254, by Donna Thakadipuram, Jordan Waggoner, Shelby Hiens, Megan Culler, and Daniel Ricci, is a cybersecurity incident response guide. It was written specifically for wind energy. Wind farms run distributed industrial control systems across remote sites. A generic office IT playbook fits them poorly. This guide tailors response roles, triggers, and procedures to wind plant operations.

Incident categories are spelled out in operational terms. They include outages that hit customers, suspicious files or malicious code on production servers, and phishing aimed at distributed wind users. Spear phishing against staff with high-level privileges is covered too. For each, the guide assigns responsibilities across analysts, engineers, technicians, farm managers, service providers, and regulators. A small operator can see who acts, who decides, and who must be informed during an event.
doe-osti-3022412-powering-progress-incre:
A final technical report from the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies, coordinated by Meaghan Gade under DOE award DE-EE0010759. It covers a year of work helping state fish and wildlife agencies take part in writing nationwide wildlife guidelines for utility-scale solar farms. Solar buildout is moving fast, and states hold much of the wildlife expertise and authority, but they needed support to stay engaged in an industry-led process.

From March 2024 to February 2025 the association convened the state agencies and documented their priorities. It also provided logistical and technical backing for their part in the process. A Solar Communications Framework, built around early and repeated communication between developers and agencies, was adopted by the association's membership and now organizes the ongoing work. By the grant's end the full guidelines were in late-stage development with state priorities largely folded in.
doe-osti-3022420-navigating-integration-:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-87663, by Paul Talbot and eight colleagues, examines what it will take to plug fast-growing data centers into a power system that includes nuclear generation. Data centers are projected to consume 6.7 to 12 percent of United States electricity by 2028, driven by artificial intelligence and cloud demand, while nuclear plants offer firm baseload power but move on slower siting and licensing timelines.

The report works stakeholder by stakeholder: data centers need speed and uptime, utilities face a flood of large-load interconnection requests, and nuclear providers must handle siting, ramping, and regulation. Grid risks are concrete, including an ERCOT review finding more than 30 near-miss events since 2020 in which large loads disconnected suddenly. Collaboration strategies close the report, tied to federal AI and energy initiatives.
doe-osti-3024494-rigid-mode-limit-of-the: Particle accelerators steer beams of protons at nearly the speed of light, and keeping those beams stable is pure math. This paper simplifies two well-known formulas used to predict beam wobble, working out what happens in a clean limiting case. The result gives accelerator physicists a quicker way to check designs.

from-isolation-to-leadership-revised-a-r:
Latane reviews how American foreign policy outgrew isolation. He separates that policy from the Monroe Doctrine. Washington and Jefferson, he argues, opposed permanent alliances, not all action abroad. The early chapters trace the Doctrine's formulation. Later ones test it against the European balance of power.

The second half follows America's widening role. Latane covers the open-door policy and relations with Britain. He treats Pan-Americanism and the failure of neutrality. War aims, the Treaty of Versailles, and the Washington Conference close the book. The revised edition brings the story into the 1920s. Latane writes as a historian judging policy, not a partisan. His case is that leadership had replaced isolation in fact.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KSFO_KSFO:
Harold Weisberg wrote on February 27, 1968 to a man named Jack in San Francisco. The letter reports his radio appearances on the coast. It also covers Jim Garrison's subpoena of Allen Dulles, the former CIA director, and interviews Weisberg had conducted with men named Hell and Howard.

A subpoena aimed at a former director of Central Intelligence was Garrison at his boldest, and Weisberg followed it closely. The letter mixes the researcher's two lives: broadcasting his case by day, working sources by mail. It preserves both, three weeks into a very public investigation.
how-to-use-your-mind-a-psychology-of-stu:
Harry Dexter Kitson, a psychology professor at Indiana University, wrote this study manual in 1921. Its subject is supervised study, for students and teachers alike. College, Kitson argues, is not the most strategic point for such training. Habits of application set earlier, in high school and the grades.

Obscurity in reading starts most lapses of attention, he finds. A hard thought, a vague sentence, or one strange word hazes the meaning. The mind then drifts to an easier channel, he writes. Kitson teaches readers to trace and block that drift. Schools running methods-of-study classes got a text built for their exact need.
nasa-tm-19660006060-waste-management-and:
Extended crewed missions cannot throw waste away, so this report works through waste management and personal hygiene in a sealed spacecraft. Its contents move from the problem itself to techniques of collection and transport. Storage, processing and reclamation, and final rejection each receive a full section. System designs are then built by joining those pieces in different ways.

Personal hygiene closes the plan, from oral care to shaving and showering. Long flights to distant targets were the design case. A crew's health and morale rest on such unglamorous systems working quietly. The report shows mission planning at its most practical, where daily life must be engineered like any engine.
nasa-tm-19660014385-a-comparison-of-two-:
Robert B Owen at Marshall compared two greenhouse models of the Venus atmosphere in a December 4, 1963, report. Cytherean is an older name for Venus and its air. A greenhouse model explains how the air traps heat and makes the surface far hotter than sunlight alone would. Carl Sagan had proposed both the original model and a newer one, Owen notes.

Recent measurements of water vapor, by Spinrad, fit the original idea, Owen reports. The newer model points to surface conditions more extreme than had been suspected. Owen builds his comparison from a survey of the literature. Before any probe landed, models like these were the only guide to the Venus surface.
nasa-tm-19670016747-fundamentals-of-sele:
Koichi Masubuchi and R. E. Keith, of the Battelle Memorial Institute, wrote this report in January 1967 under an Army contract. Distributed through the Redstone Scientific Information Center in Alabama, it surveys what was then known about how adhesive-bonded joints deform and fail. The same questions cover the thin interface where metal meets adhesive.

The survey's first chapter covers theoretical and experimental stress analyses of bonded joints, plus their flow behavior over time. Fracture, and the effects of loading and environment on deformation, get full treatment, as do design and fabrication problems. A second chapter turns to the atom-level mechanisms by which metal-adhesive interfaces deform. The closing chapter draws conclusions and recommends directions for future research. The authors note the survey was written to assist another investigation in the same field.
nasa-tm-19680014424-calculation-of-captu:
John V. Dugan Jr. and James H. Rice of Lewis Research Center, with John L. Magee of the University of Notre Dame, calculated collision rates for ions and polar molecules in this May 1968 report. Their test case was methyl cyanide, a symmetric top molecule written CH3CN. Such collisions react strongly, so their capture rates matter to chemists.

The team computed the capture cross sections with numbers rather than simple formulas. Adding the molecule's rotational freedom changed the results in clear ways. The values fell below the top classical limit but stayed far above the older Langevin values. When the results were combined over energy, they agreed well with what the paper reports from prior work.
nasa-tm-19680024875-an-analysis-of-blade:
Julian L. Jenkins Jr. of Langley Research Center analyzes blade motion stability for articulated helicopter rotors in this May 1968 paper. A fully articulated rotor lets each blade flap and move in lead-lag motion. Jenkins solves the coupled nonlinear equations of motion numerically to judge stability.

Two effects of starting conditions on the divergence limit are examined. He varies where the disturbance begins around the rotor's rotation. He also varies the disturbance size at the critical azimuth angle. Methods to extend the divergence boundary are then tested. Hinge restraint from springs and damping is weighed, as is flapping hinge cant angle. A representative combination of these fixes is also evaluated.
nasa-tm-19720008259-comparison-of-temper:
Herbert J Gladden, John N B Livingood, and Daniel J Gauntner of the Lewis Research Center compared two test worlds in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2477. Their subject was a finned turbine vane cooled by air jets and an air film. One data set came from a still four vane cascade in a laboratory. The other came from a real research gas turbine engine. Designers needed to know if cheap cascade tests told the truth.

The cascade ran gas at heat up to twenty two hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit. Its pressure reached eighty pounds per square inch. The team recorded average and local metal temperatures in both settings. They then matched the temperature patterns in several ways. Agreement would validate cascade testing for future cooled vane work.
nasa-tm-19720011337-remote-evaluation-of:
Victor L Coles of NASA presented this paper in September 1971 at a forum on interactive bibliographic systems. The forum met at the National Bureau of Standards in Washington. Coles described how NASA judged its own literature search service, NASA RECON. RECON let users at remote consoles search technical literature interactively. NASA wanted steady feedback from the people actually using it. The paper runs to twenty nine pages.

The method was simple and direct. An evaluation form went out with every literature search performed. Users returned their judgments along with the results. The report explains the technique in full. It also presents the findings drawn from those returned forms. The work is an early study of user satisfaction with online searching.
outlines-of-universal-history-designed-a:
George Park Fisher, a Yale professor, designed his Outlines of Universal History as a textbook for advanced pupils and for private reading. In his preface he lists what such a book should do. It should present the essential facts in due order. Those facts should follow the best and latest research. The book should show how events and eras connect. Illustrative incidents should relieve the dryness of a mere summary.

It should also, Fisher insists, be free from sectarian partiality and limit itself to well-established judgments on contested matters. Writing it impressed on him more than ever the unity of history — the great, deeply moving drama still advancing into a hidden future. He hopes that feeling communicates itself to the reader page by page.

podcast-tuckercarlson-N3z_kpaLmFo:
Rob O'Neill, the Navy SEAL credited with killing Osama bin Laden, shares shocking stories from SEAL Team 6 with Tucker Carlson. O'Neill's years in the elite unit took him through America's hardest missions. Here he also tells politicians what they should know before starting wars.

quotes-and-images-from-the-tales-and-nov:
Quotes and Images from the Tales and Novels of Jean de La Fontaine gathers the tale-teller's sharpest lines. They stand in alphabetical order. A short life of La Fontaine follows them. He was born on July 8, 1621, at Château-Thierry. His family held a respectable position there.

The extracts warn the reader with a pretty wife to beware the monks as he would guard his life, and hold that above all law is might. Delays are dangerous in love or war, extremes in everything soonest tire, and the god of love and wisdom never agree. We scarcely find good without alloy, the tales conclude, in their worldly, smiling way.

the-lake-of-the-sky-lake-tahoe-in-the-hi:
George Wharton James devoted this volume to Lake Tahoe. The lake lies in the high Sierras of California and Nevada. L. C. Page and Company of Boston published it in 1915. James had written Arizona, the Wonderland and other western books. The subtitle is a contents list in itself. The lake's history, Indians, and discovery by Frémont appear. Legendary lore, various namings, and glacial features follow. Geology, automobile routes, and historic towns come next. Early mining excitements, the steamer ride, and mineral springs fill it out.

The book carries a map and sixty-five plates. A folding panorama is among them. James adds a full account of the Tahoe National Forest and its waters. He dedicates the volume to Robert M. Watson. Bob is fearless explorer, expert mountaineer, and peerless guide. Truthful fisherman, humane hunter, and delightful raconteur follow. The dedication sets the book's hearty, boosterish tone.
